B000490.text: This week, I asked the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, to explain how poorly planned cuts to the federal workforce last year have weakened services and protections upon which Americans rely. This includes the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, which is responsible for protecting America’s agriculture from invasive species and diseases. USDA-APHIS began mounting a vigorous response to the resurgence of New World Screwworm – a deadly parasite affecting livestock – in 2024. However, in early 2025, the Administration illegally fired workers and forced others to resign, causing over 25 percent of all USDA-APHIS employees to leave. USDA’s New World Screwworm prevention, monitoring, surveillance, and control efforts were halted. USDA had approved $378 million in prevention and control funding for sterile fly facilities in 2023 and 2024, yet the money went unspent when the new administration paused funding. This is extremely concerning to our ranchers, and this outbreak could drive the price of food even higher. Unfortunately, we continue to see the fallout of the blunt and ill-considered cuts to federal workers, from the return of New World Screwworm to the United States, to farmers showing up to closed or understaffed Farm Service Agency offices, to attacks on our nuclear safety programs putting national security at risk. I will continue to hold the White House accountable, as I did this week during the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government hearing with Mr. Vought.

Today, Congressman Austin Scott (GA-08) and I testified before the U.S. House Natural Resources Subcommittee on Federal Lands regarding our bipartisan bill, the Ocmulgee Mounds National Park Redesignation Act (H.R. 9416). As our nation prepares to celebrate its 250th birthday this Saturday, it is vital that we preserve and protect our ancient history, including the stories of the indigenous peoples who lived here long before July 4, 1776. Our bill today represents a small, albeit meaningful, step forward that will strengthen Ocmulgee and ensure that its cultural and religious sites are protected now and into the future. This continues a more than decade long, but steady and combined effort of local, state, and federal leaders to create Georgia’s first National Park and more closely realize the original vision for this historic and cultural treasure which will also bring more visitors and jobs to Middle Georgia.

The National Fish and Wildlife Foundation recently awarded $20 million for projects that will restore and protect longleaf pine forests in Georgia. Terrorists. Cartels. Human traffickers. Drug smugglers. Each day, ICE and Border Patrol agents and officers confront these threats head-on to keep America safe. C001063.text: Housing costs remain one of the biggest challenges facing families in South Texas. As http://Realtor.com reported, new-home sales have slowed, builders are being cautious with new construction, and mortgage rates remain high. When fewer homes are being built and borrowing costs stay high, it becomes harder for families to find a home they can afford. That is why I voted to pass the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. This bill takes practical steps to cut unnecessary delays, support new housing construction, improve federal housing programs, and help expand affordable housing. No single bill will fix the housing market overnight, but increasing housing supply is an important part of lowering costs. I will continue working with both parties to make housing more affordable for families in #TX28. https://www.mysanantonio.com/realestate/article/congress-aims-to-lower-housing-costs-with-new-22322752.php

A construction site should not be sitting empty because workers are afraid to show up. Families in South Texas need housing, businesses need workers, and our communities need projects like this to move forward. I have long supported strong border security, but enforcement should be targeted at criminals and real threats to public safety. When workers are scared, projects get delayed, costs go up, and local economies feel it. We need smart, targeted enforcement that keeps our communities safe without hurting the workers, families, and businesses that help build South Texas.

Big news for Laredo and South Texas: I secured a $25,000,000 federal BUILD grant for the World Trade Bridge Expansion Project. This is a major investment for the most important trade crossing in the country. The World Trade Bridge supports jobs, commerce, and supply chains across South Texas and the nation, and this funding will help make sure our infrastructure keeps up with growing trade. The project will add two lanes to the existing bridge and construct a new, separate span with eight northbound lanes, helping reduce congestion and strengthen the movement of goods through Laredo and Webb County. A formal announcement with Mayor Dr. Victor Treviño and the Laredo City Council will follow. I’ll continue delivering federal dollars to #TX28 and support the infrastructure projects that keep South Texas moving.

When I was first elected to the Minnesota House, our offices sat next door to one another, and we shared a Legislative Assistant. Together, we worked to pass Minnesota's landmark Human Rights Act, and in 2013 she authored the legislation that made Minnesota the 12th state to legalize marriage equality. M001153.text: The Supreme Court’s decision today recognizes that states face unique circumstances in administering their elections. In Alaska, voting is not as simple as driving down the road to a neighborhood polling place. Many Alaskans live in remote communities that are not connected to the road system, requiring ballots to travel by bush plane or boat, which means volatile weather conditions and limited infrastructure can determine whether those ballots arrive on time. Even with Alaska’s current 10-day grace period for in-state ballots, we have seen mail delays cause legally cast ballots to arrive too late to be counted. Today’s decision affirms that states have the flexibility to account for these realities and helps ensure that every American who lawfully casts a ballot has the opportunity to have it counted. https://apnews.com/article/supreme-court-mailed-ballots-trump-elections-5f24f718ea92a33838485ce6302e079e

Team Peters has lost a talented and tenacious member of our alumni family after a years-long battle with cancer. Kelly Davis was an award-winning journalist who served as our Press Secretary from 2023-2024. For several years before she joined the office, we admired Kelly’s skill in writing stories that made a difference for our region – about homelessness, housing affordability, and criminal justice reform. Investigative reporting was her calling, and her work led to new state laws that have made California a more just and transparent place for everyone. It was an honor that she came to work with us. We appreciated the history, depth, and context she brought to the role of Press Secretary, as well as the kind, compassionate demeanor she brought to the team. We learned from her quiet maturity. She taught us more about how journalism and storytelling work and we taught her a little about how government ought to function; we gained invaluable insights from each other. Today, we’re especially remembering our staff retreat in Washington, D.C. that year. She was a lot of fun on that trip! When she felt called back to journalism, we understood and knew that she would continue to shine a light on injustice and give a voice to those who needed it. She did just that for as long as she could. Our community has lost a trusted source of information and a fierce advocate for change. We will miss her deeply and send Kelly’s loved ones our warmest condolences.

C001098.text: Today’s decision is a major victory for the First Amendment. Political parties exist to advance ideas, support candidates, and persuade voters. Their speech does not lose constitutional protection because they coordinate with the candidates they nominate. The Federalist Papers cost money to print. Common Sense cost money to distribute. Modern political advocacy costs money to communicate. Congress cannot ration core political speech. The Court got it right.

Today’s decision regarding birthright citizenship is a travesty. The Fourteenth Amendment was written to overturn Dred Scott and guarantee citizenship to freed slaves—not to create automatic citizenship for the children of those who violate our immigration laws or are only temporarily in the United States. This decision will only invite further exploitation of our immigration system. The Court adopted an interpretation that departs from the original meaning of the Constitution and incentivizes illegal immigration. Congress retains the authority to clarify federal law, and it should act immediately to restore the original meaning of the Citizenship Clause and protect the integrity of American citizenship.

Today’s Supreme Court decision is a victory for the plain language of the Constitution. Article II vests all executive authority in the President, and Congress cannot constitutionally prohibit the President from dismissing executive branch employees. I have long predicted that the Court would overrule Humphrey’s Executor—which was wrongly decided on the day it was issued—and that’s exactly what a 6-3 majority just did.

F000466.text: 250 years ago, in Philadelphia, our Founders gathered to declare a truth that would change the course of history: that our rights come not from government, but from God; that all are created equal; and that liberty is both America’s inheritance and America’s calling. Today, I had the profound honor of standing in their footsteps at Independence Hall, alongside a bipartisan delegation of my colleagues and Governor Shapiro, to deliver the opening invocation as our nation prepares to mark America’s 250th year. To stand in that hallowed hall— where an idea became a Declaration, where conviction became a Republic, and where the work of America began—was a moment I will never forget. At this historic threshold, may we look back with gratitude and forward with renewed commitment to the sacred charge entrusted to every generation: to remain one people, bound by one Republic, and called to carry America’s promise forward together. My sincere thanks to my friends and partners, @CongBoyle and @RepJeffries, for the hosting this historic occasion.

Today in Historic Bristol Borough, we honored one of the quiet beginnings of the American story. In 1775, before our independence was won and before our Constitution was written, the Second Continental Congress established a national postal system under Benjamin Franklin, our first Postmaster General. Bristol was chosen as one of the original 61 Postal Service offices—a vital link on the route between Philadelphia and New York at a time when communication was not a convenience, but a lifeline for liberty. Through revolution and reunion, war and peace, hardship and prosperity, the Bristol Borough Post Office has carried more than mail. It has carried news from home, word from the front, notices of birth and loss, commerce for small businesses, and the daily threads that bind neighbors, families, and a nation together. That is the beauty of this anniversary. It reminds us that America was built not only by the names etched in marble, but by generations of citizens and public servants who did their duty faithfully, quietly, and well. For 250 years, the men and women of the Bristol Borough Post Office have served this community with dedication and pride. And across our nation, postal workers continue that same essential mission every day, connecting Americans from the largest cities to the smallest towns, from one doorstep to the next. As we continue marching towards America’s 250th birthday, please join me in thanking every incredible postal worker who has served Historic Bristol Borough across these two and a half centuries, and all of America’s postal workers who continue to keep our communities, our commerce, and our country connected. Their service is honorable, and their legacy is deeply American.

I joined my friend and bipartisan partner @RepGoodlander on Meet the Press to discuss our first-of-its-kind Public Service Accountability Act. After introducing the Restore Trust in Congress Act earlier this year to ban Members of Congress from trading individual stocks, this new legislation takes the next step: one clear ethics standard for senior officials across Congress, the executive branch, and the federal judiciary. The principle is simple: public office is a public trust. Those with access to sensitive information and the power to shape policy should not be trading individual stocks, participating in prediction markets, or using positions of public service for personal financial gain. The American people deserve a government that serves them—not itself. Watch our full conversation below ⬇️:

RT by @RepLangworthy: America at 250. July 2 is one of my favorite dates because of John Adams. July 2, 1786, the delegates are exhausted, the debates have dragged on for weeks, and the weight of history presses down like the summer humidity. On this very day, July 2, 1776, Adams and his allies push the Continental Congress to vote for independence from Great Britain. The resolution passes. The colonies are no longer subjects; they are free, or at least determined to become so. Adams writes to his beloved Abigail that day: “The Second Day of July 1776, will be the most memorable Epocha, in the History of America… It ought to be solemnized with Pomp and Parade, with Shews, Games, Sports, Guns, Bells, Bonfires and Illuminations from one End of this Continent to the other from this Time forward forever more.” He was off by two days. July 4 would get the glory when the Declaration was formally adopted, but he nailed the spirit. As we race toward America 250 in 2026, this moment feels electric. Two hundred fifty years ago, a group of imperfect but courageous people bet everything on the radical idea that governments derive their power from the consent of the governed. They chose hope over fear, unity over division, and liberty over submission. Today is all about John Adams!

On this day in 1944, over 34,000 American soldiers crowded together in small, amphibious boats en route to Omaha Beach. As the boats landed on the beach, and their bow ramps dropped down leading the men ashore, unrelenting machine gun fire rained down from enemy bunkers. Undeterred, the American and Allied forces emerged from the battle victorious, but not without a heavy cost. Over 2,500 Americans died at Omaha Beach. One of them was 1st Lieutenant Thomas Royce Dallas Jr. from our Congressional District in Griffin, Georgia, who drew his last breath on the shores of Omaha Beach. As we remember the heroism Americans exhibited on D-Day and we reflect on the cost of freedom, may we remember and be inspired by the names and faces of those brave soldiers who died in service to our Country.

The Supreme Court has now issued its decision on birthright citizenship, resolving one of the most significant constitutional cases before the Court this term. I hope this provides a straightforward overview of the decision and its broader legal significance.
